passages.t: Far be it from God to do wrong
passages.happening:
‘Then Elihu continued’ (verse 1). “Hear my words, O wise men; give ear to me, O men of learning. For the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food” (verses 2-3).

Job has said that he is righteous and that God has taken away his justice. “What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water?” (verse 7). He keeps company with evildoers, Elihu says, and claims that it profits a man nothing to delight in God.

“Therefore listen to me, O men of understanding. Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly” (verse 10). God repays each person for what they do. “Who gave Him charge over the earth? Who appointed Him over the whole world? If He were to set His heart to it and withdraw His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust” (verses 13-15).
passages.hearers:
This is Elihu's second speech. In chapter 33 he spoke to Job, gently at first. Now he turns to a wider audience, the wise men of the circle, and his tone hardens. He frames the speech as a public hearing, and he casts Job almost as a defendant. He even quotes a saying Job himself had used (12:11).

His target is the charge at the center of Job's complaint, that God has treated an innocent man unjustly. Where the three friends defended God by accusing Job of hidden sin, Elihu defends God chiefly by describing who God is. God owes his office to no one. He holds every living thing in being by his breath. Why would such a God need to pervert justice?

Keeping company with evildoers was a serious charge in a world built on honor and reputation, where a man was known by the company he kept.
passages.later: A psalm says the same of every creature's breath: “When You hide Your face, they are terrified; when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust” (Psalm 104:29).
passages.hard:
Is Elihu fair to Job when he says Job claims there is no profit in delighting in God?

Not entirely. Job never quite said that of himself. He did describe the wicked as asking what they would gain by praying to the Almighty (21:15), and he did say that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike (9:22). Elihu seems to have gathered Job's words into their most damaging form.

Some interpreters think this is a fair summary: Job's protest, pressed to its end, implies that goodness does not pay. Others see it as the same failure the friends showed, hearing a sufferer's anguish as blasphemy. Elihu is right that God does not pervert justice, and the book agrees. But the reader knows from the prologue why Job is suffering, and Elihu does not.
passages.asks: Elihu put Job's words in their worst light. Ask whether you have ever done that with someone who spoke out of pain. And ask how you can defend what is true about God without condemning the one who is struggling to believe it.

passages.t: The ruler who shows no favor
passages.happening:
“If you have understanding, hear this; listen to my words. Could one who hates justice govern?” (verses 16-17). God says to kings that they are worthless and to nobles that they are wicked. He ‘is not partial to princes and does not favor rich over poor? For they are all the work of His hands’ (verse 19). The mighty die in a moment, in the night.

‘For His eyes are on the ways of a man, and He sees his every step. There is no darkness or deep shadow where the workers of iniquity can hide’ (verses 21-22). God shatters the mighty and sets up others in their place. They oppressed the poor, ‘and He heard the outcry of the afflicted’ (verse 28).

“But when He remains silent, who can condemn Him? When He hides His face, who can see Him?” (verse 29). Yet he watches over nations and people, so that the godless do not rule.
passages.hearers:
Behind the passage stands an ideal common across the ancient Near East: the ruler as guardian of justice. Kings described themselves as defenders of the weak, and Israel's psalms and prophets expected the same of its kings. Elihu applies the ideal to God and raises it higher. Earthly kings owe their office to someone; God to no one. Earthly kings favor the rich; God favors no one. Earthly kings fall suddenly, sometimes in the night, and God is the one who removes them.

To call a king worthless or a noble wicked to his face was unthinkable for a subject. Only a higher power could do it.

Verse 29 is honest. Elihu admits that God sometimes stays silent and hides his face, the very thing Job has complained of. His answer is that no one can condemn God for it.
passages.later: The law says the same of God: ‘the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe’ (Deuteronomy 10:17).
passages.asks: Elihu said God hears the cry of the poor and favors no one. Ask whether you treat the powerful and the powerless the same. And ask whose cry you have not heard.

passages.happening:
Elihu imagines someone saying to God that he has borne his punishment and will not offend again, and asking God to teach him what he cannot see. “Should God repay you on your own terms when you have disavowed His? You must choose, not I; so tell me what you know” (verse 33).

Then he turns to the wise men for a verdict. They will say, he claims, that Job speaks without knowledge. “If only Job were tried to the utmost for answering like a wicked man. For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God” (verses 36-37).
passages.hearers:
Elihu's question in verse 33 is whether Job can set the terms of God's justice. It is a fair question, and God himself will put something like it to Job (40:8).

But by the end of the chapter Elihu has joined the friends in condemning Job. Clapping the hands was a gesture of scorn or defiance, the opposite of respectful silence before a superior. Elihu wishes that Job's testing would go further.

The phrase without knowledge in verse 35 will return. God's first words from the whirlwind ask who darkens counsel ‘by words without knowledge’ (38:2).
passages.asks: Elihu wished Job's testing would go on. Ask whether you have ever wished someone's suffering would teach them a lesson. And ask whether that wish came from love or from wanting to be proved right.
